latest_articles.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
latest_articles.title: Transition to Parenthood and Changes in Wellbeing and Relationship Quality: A Propensity Score Matching Approach
latest_articles.abstract: Does becoming a parent enhance or undermine wellbeing and relationship quality? Mixed findings along with methodological challenges do not provide clear answers. Drawing from nationally representative data in New Zealand collected across 2012–2024, we extended prior studies by using propensity score matching to compare changes in both wellbeing and relationship quality of people who became parents ( n = 1,260) to matched controls who did not become parents ( n = 1,260) but were similar in key socio-demographics and baseline wellbeing and relationship quality. On average, parenthood had small wellbeing benefits. Matched controls experienced small steady declines in life satisfaction and increases in psychological distress. By contrast, people who became parents sustained higher life satisfaction for 2 years following the transition before declining to the same levels as matched controls 4 years later. New parents also did not show increases in psychological distress, but differences to matched controls were small and mostly nonsignificant. Parenthood was also accompanied by relationship challenges. Both matched controls and people who became parents experienced significant declines in relationship satisfaction across time, and these trajectories did not significantly differ. However, new parents reported significantly stronger increases in conflict across the following 4 years compared to matched controls. The results strengthen evidence that parents may experience small life satisfaction benefits, and indicate that declines in relationship satisfaction may not be as unique to the transition to parenthood as prior studies assume, but reveal that new parents may encounter increases in relationship conflict that likely challenge relationship satisfaction and wellbeing.

latest_articles.title: Contesting the infrastructures of attention: Climate activism and asymmetric visibility in France
latest_articles.abstract: Drawing on two years of ethnographic fieldwork with Extinction Rebellion Paris and allied movements, semi-structured interviews with activists, and analysis of media coverage and investigative reporting on police surveillance technology, this article examines how French climate movements have reoriented their political practice from seeking visibility within an existing media system toward contesting the infrastructures of attention through which public visibility is produced and governed. It argues that this reorientation reflects a shift in the politics of climate communication: from a logic of media access to one of infrastructural contestation, targeting media ownership and security apparatuses. The analysis examines how activists experience narratives of disorder and eco-terrorism as challenges to their political legitimacy, alongside the expansion of biometric surveillance documented by investigative reporting. It develops the concept of asymmetric visibility regimes to capture the resulting double bind, in which activists struggle for recognition in the media sphere while becoming increasingly identifiable in the security sphere. The article contributes to debates on media power, hybrid media systems, and the communicative conditions of democratic dissent.
affiliations: Albert Hirschman Centre on Democracy, Geneva Graduate Institute (Institut de hautes études internationales et du développement, IHEID), Switzerland

latest_articles.title: Testing Hypotheses From the Social Approval Theory of Online Hate: An Analysis of 110 Million Messages From Parler
latest_articles.abstract: We examined how social approval motivates online hate via the social approval theory, which argues social approval signals on hate messages predict (1) more hate speech, and (2) more toxicity. Using 110 million messages from Parler (2018–2021), we observed that upvotes on hate speech posts (messages broadcast on users’ profiles to followers’ feeds) predicted a lower probability of hate speech in the next immediate post but more in the following week’s posts. Additionally, upvotes on comments (messages embedded within conversational threads) negatively predicted hate speech in the next comment but positively predicted the degree of toxicity during the next week and month. Between-person effects revealed negative immediate short-term effects but positive longer-term effects for hate speech. For comments , social disapproval (downvotes) moderated these relationships, making them less positive at weekly through quarterly time-intervals and more strongly negative at 6-months. Social approval predicts online hate in time- and message-dependent ways.
affiliations: Michigan State University, East Lansing, USA

latest_articles.title: Complicating “Good” Grief: A Collaborative Motherwriting of Pregnancy Loss
latest_articles.abstract: This essay navigates the tensions of grief surrounding pregnancy loss, specifically miscarriage, by employing collaborative motherwriting as both methodological and epistemological inquiry. We disrupt dominant discourses of “good grief” as dry, private, and contained through layered collaborative motherwriting autoethnographic vignettes. Our assemblage of vignettes and cultural critiques foreground the radical specificity of our pregnancy loss experiences and reveal the complex textures of grief—private yet public, leaky yet contained, and linear yet erratic. We complicate the cultural scripting of miscarriage as a private and isolated experience. As academic mothers negotiating cultural differences and academic expectations, we resist linearity and predictability; instead, we embrace the messy and fragmented temporality and emotional leakage that grief demands. Our hope is that this essay might evoke more ways to communicate about pregnancy loss in everyday conversations and to unpack the complex, nonlinear realities of grief for bereaved mothers and for those in their support network.

latest_articles.title: Dyadic Trajectories of Financial Behaviors in Marriage: Predictors, Consequences, and Structural Disparities
latest_articles.abstract: This study investigates the joint developmental trajectories of financial behaviors, their predictors, and outcomes within the first decade of marriage. We used Waves 2–7 (six waves) of dyadic data from 1505 different‐gender couples. Growth curve analyses showed that healthy financial behaviors continued to increase but began declining between Wave 5 (April 2021–December 2021) and Wave 6 (April 2022–December 2022), coinciding with economic challenges at the time. Latent profile analyses identified three subgroups: “moderate momenta with fades” (P1, 40.3%), “peaking and ebbing” (P2, 36.3%), and “stalling in shallows” (P3, 23.5%). P1 and P2 were associated with higher relational commitment than P3. Socioeconomic inequalities were the key predictors. Higher education and household income were associated with higher likelihoods of the more adaptive P1 and P2 (compared to P3). Wives' longer working hours and husbands' prior marriage were linked to a lower likelihood of P2 than P3. P2 was more likely (than P1) when household income and wives' education were higher, but less likely when wives worked longer hours or husbands had a prior marriage. Our study advances family finance research by demonstrating how couples' financial behaviors co‐evolve and highlights the urgent need for financial interventions, particularly among socioeconomically marginalized populations.
affiliations: Department of Applied Social Sciences The Hong Kong Polytechnic University Hong Kong Hong Kong SAR China
Department of Social Work The Chinese University of Hong Kong Hong Kong Hong Kong SAR China
Institute for Disability Research, Policy & Practice Utah State University Logan Utah USA
School of Family Life Brigham Young University Provo Utah USA

latest_articles.title: Do Experts Agree About Misinformation? Evidence From Three Annual Surveys
latest_articles.abstract: How much do experts on the information environment agree about the scale, spread, and effects of misinformation? We drew on three annual waves of the International Panel on the Information Environment expert survey to examine agreement with seven popular claims about misinformation (2023: N = 262; 2024: N = 413; 2025: N = 442; spanning 76 countries). Agreement varied widely across statements and was stable across waves. About 60% of experts agreed that falsehoods spread faster than the truth and that misinformation is widespread. About half agreed that misinformation has a substantial influence on behavior and that people readily believe what they see online; about 40% agreed that more people have become misinformed over time; and only 25% agreed that misinformation is primarily a social media problem. The surveys also revealed a persistent divide between experts who saw misinformation as widespread and consequential and those more skeptical, with sharpest disagreement on its behavioral impact and increase over time. In 2025, some experts distinguished between misperception prevalence and misinformation severity. Overall agreement varied by respondent background: agreement was higher among experts on developing countries than those on developed countries, higher among STEM researchers than social scientists, and lower among political scientists than communication scholars. Expert consensus on misinformation is partial, varies across claims and experts, and is shaped by geography and discipline.
affiliations: Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile, Santiago, Chile

latest_articles.title: Exploring the Predictors and Outcomes of Perceived Algorithm Responsiveness in Social Media Feeds: Combining Longitudinal and Computational Methods
latest_articles.abstract: Perceptions of how algorithms curate content are integral to how people use social media and its effects. Building on the algorithm responsiveness process, we explore whether perceived algorithm responsiveness (PAR) was associated with the message cues of algorithmically curated content. We coupled longitudinal data from a 7-day, twice-daily diary survey with computational digital traces from Twitter (now X) to operationalize algorithmic message characteristics and to understand the antecedents and outcomes of PAR ( N = 10,337 tweets). Results suggested that message cues from algorithmic content in social feeds (i.e., closeness, popularity, valence, and format) were associated with perceived message personalization, but message personalization was the only message characteristic associated with PAR. PAR predicted feeling more connected to others on Twitter, along with message-level factors: closeness to the poster and message personalization. This work contributes to the algorithm responsiveness process, demonstrating that characteristics of algorithmically curated messages predict how individuals experience algorithms.
affiliations: Michigan State University, East Lansing, USA

latest_articles.title: When it’s your own child: effects of media narratives on U.S. parents’ support for their LGBTQ+ teen
latest_articles.abstract: Parents’ responses to their LGBTQ+ child are varied, often intense, and have important consequences for the child. To examine how media depictions may shape responses, a pre-registered online experiment of 494 parents tested effects of viewing two TV narratives, depicting either control (non-LGBTQ+) family interactions, parental rejection, gradual growth toward acceptance, or unalloyed acceptance, of a lesbian or transgender teen, on parents’ support and behavioral intentions regarding their own LGBTQ+ teen. Guided by theories of vicarious contact and inspiring media, we assessed mediation via identification with characters, and via feelings of inspiration and manipulation, testing baseline support as a moderator. Effects of condition were indirect-only, and contingent on baseline support. Among highly supportive parents, growth and acceptance narratives (vs. control) increased feelings of inspiration, which predicted positive behavioral intentions. Among less supportive parents, rejection and (unexpectedly) growth narratives reduced identification with depicted LGBTQ+ teens, indirectly decreasing support and behavioral intentions.
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison Department of Communication Arts, , Madison, WI 53706,
Stanford University Social Media Lab & Tech Impact and Policy Center, , Stanford, CA 94305,

latest_articles.title: Promoting Support for Anti-Racism Movements and Intentions to Intervene: Effects of Common-Identity Narratives and the Moderating Role of Prior Prejudice
latest_articles.abstract: Two experiments examined whether emphasizing a common ingroup identity with racially different characters, operationalized as university affiliation with an African American character (Study 1) and parent identity with an Asian American character (Study 2), enhanced the impact of victim narratives. Findings indicate that emphasizing a common ingroup identity increased perceived similarity and identification with the character and reduced perceived social distance, which then fostered greater support toward anti-racism movements and stronger intentions to intervene. Common-identity narratives were particularly effective among participants with higher prior prejudice, and the moderation effect was mediated by reduced social distance.

latest_articles.title: AI for the audiences: Envisioning the future media environment
latest_articles.abstract: The rapid development and broad-ranging deployment of generative AI poses significant repercussions for media and journalism. Media research has primarily concentrated on newsroom applications, while the potential use of AI by audiences remains underexplored. Drawing on theoretical lenses from media and communication studies, we examine how generative AI in media consumption may drive a shift in the media and information environment. Our empirical study with 17 researcher participants employs design fictions to explore this shift. We analyse and discuss the envisioned development in terms of potential changes in media consumption, audience relationship and key information concerns, with implications for media processes and journalist roles, audience agency, media business models and societal engagement.

latest_articles.title: Unfinished becoming: Seriality, temporality, and the making of literature on Wenxuecity
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines Wenxuecity, a long-running website for overseas Chinese communities, as a site of diasporic literary production shaped by distinctive temporal practices. Drawing on the serialized fiction of two active contributors and sustained observation of forum discussions, it identifies three intertwined temporalities: narrative, processual, and archival. Narrative temporality foregrounds authors’ self-directed rhythms of storytelling; processual temporality traces how ongoing exchanges between authors and readers turn writing into a collective, open-ended practice; and archival temporality reveals how dispersed texts accumulate into a layered record of diasporic becoming. The article argues that these temporal practices sustain a mode of digital cultural production oriented toward continuity, participation, and lived experience—one that contests the extractive logics of platform economies rather than merely operating within them. As a fragile media archive, Wenxuecity holds cultural memory in the constitutive tension between accumulation and precarity.

latest_articles.title: “Gender essentialism is cringe”: Brazilian and Ukrainian queer players’ strategies for queering character interactions
latest_articles.abstract: This article presents the strategies that Brazilian transgender and gender diverse (TGD) players use to queer character interactions and accommodate diverse gender identities into video games, and aims to show the differences in queering strategies between Brazilian and Ukrainian players. Reflexive thematic analysis was used on survey data gathered from Brazilian and Ukrainian players. The main finding reveals the strategies for queering character interactions distinguished in Brazilian players’ responses, namely, (1) playing with an idealised self, (2) queering binary player characters, and (3) rejecting non-queerness. The results show similar ways of approaching gender binaries and treating them as queer (able), with coinciding reasoning behind. Brazilian respondents also reflected on the significance of player characters as “additional” or “alternative” bodies to experiment with, which differed from Ukrainian players seeking queerness while doubting the potential of video game spaces to accommodate their identities. The results highlight the need for further culturally informed and geographically diverse research on TGD players’ experiences in video games. The findings reflect a similar approach to gender binaries in Brazilian and Ukrainian TGD players’ experience that differs from previous research. It is also shown how bodily focused Brazilian culture makes their experiences more focused on in-game bodies.

latest_articles.title: The Emergence and Development of Dynamic Norms in Health and Environmental Communication: A Bibliometric Analysis
latest_articles.abstract: Social norms are well-established predictors of health and pro-environmental behaviors, with prior research distinguishing between descriptive and injunctive norms and between individual and collective norms. However, these distinctions largely reflect a static view of norms at a single point in time. The concept of dynamic norms addresses this limitation by incorporating temporal change, demonstrating that shifts in social norms over time can influence behavior. This perspective aligns with the reality that many recommended behaviors have not yet become widespread but are showing a positive upward trend. Despite growing empirical interest since 2017, theoretical development on dynamic norms remains limited. To map the evolution and application of this concept, we conducted a bibliometric analysis of 49 empirical articles on dynamic norms. Our findings indicated that while dynamic norms extend traditional social norm theories, the conceptualization and operationalization across studies remain inconsistent, focusing either on behavioral shifts from an old to a new behavior or on trends in the adoption of new behaviors. This review highlights the foundations and gaps in dynamic norms research and sheds light on future research on promoting health and pro-environmental behaviors.

latest_articles.title: How Chinese and U.S. media construct legitimacy at sea differently: A corpus-based comparative analysis of China’s distant-water fishing
latest_articles.abstract: Journalism plays a vital role in shaping how societies interpret and legitimize global environmental controversies. This study compares how Chinese and U.S. media discursively frame China’s distant-water fishing (DWF)—a domain where environmental, economic, and geopolitical interests intersect. Using a corpus-based mixed-method approach that integrates sentiment analysis, keyword extraction, and nomination strategies, the research analyzes 167 English-language news articles from leading outlets in both countries to uncover how legitimacy is communicatively constructed within distinct media systems. The findings reveal two coherent yet contrasting framing logics. U.S. media adopt a critical and moralized framing that emphasizes illegality, environmental harm, and systemic accountability, reflecting a liberal-institutionalist orientation rooted in watchdog journalism and rule-based governance. Chinese media, in contrast, employ a more procedural and developmental framing that highlights regulation, cooperation, and economic pragmatism, reflecting a greater emphasis on institutional coordination, policy implementation, and national development priorities. The study advances comparative journalism research by linking media framing with policy paradigms, showing how institutional and communicative contexts shape the realization of ostensibly universal news values such as Negativity and Eliteness. Methodologically, it demonstrates the value of combining computational and qualitative discourse analysis to reveal patterned differences in journalistic representation. Substantively, it underscores journalism’s dual role in global environmental discourse—as both a site where legitimacy and responsibility are contested, and a communicative bridge that may either intensify conflict or foster mutual understanding in governing shared environmental commons.

latest_articles.title: Enhancing Democratic Listening in Online Discussions: The Role of Reaction Buttons, Discussion Moderation, and Large Language Models
latest_articles.abstract: Political communication research in general – and research on political online discussions in particular – has previously focused on the exercise of democratic voice and thus largely neglected the complementary practice of democratic listening. Against the backdrop of a wide-spread perception that democratic listening is lacking in online discussions, we investigate whether listening can be strengthened through novel platform affordances. We developed an experimental online written discussion platform with listening-oriented reaction buttons and both human and AI moderation (based on GPT-4). We then conducted an experiment involving n = 740 respondents in 40 discussion groups (N = 4,355 comments), each lasting 30 minutes, covering three experimental conditions and a control condition. We compare the effect of (1) listening-oriented reaction buttons versus (2) a combination of these buttons and listening-oriented human discussion moderation versus (3) a combination of buttons and AI moderation on the level of democratic listening demonstrated in discussants’ textual contributions. We find that listening-oriented buttons alone do not enhance democratic listening. However, when combined with listening-oriented AI moderation, they are associated with a democratic listening rate of 27% within discussions, compared to 21% in the condition without either feature. Our findings lay the basis for the implementation of a combination of listening-oriented buttons and discussion moderation on news media websites, social media apps or dedicated discussion spaces using LLM-based chatbots.

latest_articles.title: Negotiating Infrastructural Integration: Cloud Services and the Evolution of News Website Ecosystems in France and the Netherlands
latest_articles.abstract: This paper analyzes the infrastructural integration of European news media with digital platforms and third-party service providers between 2015–2025. Reviewing current research, we note increased scholarly attention to the infrastructural relations between news organizations and digital platforms. Yet, despite this heightened interest, we are still missing a systematic empirical examination of how infrastructural integration shapes the spaces of negotiation between news media and tech companies. We provide such an examination through a historical analysis of the top ten news websites in France and the Netherlands, using a custom version of the 4CAT Capture and Analysis Toolkit on 9,456 archived snapshots. The analysis of evolving third-party service (de-)integrations, highlight the rise of audiovisual content and the decline of website analytics, as well as broader industry and regulatory developments (e.g., GDPR). These changes in website architectures point to shifting strategies of news organizations to adapt and preserve their independence in an online environment increasingly dominated by digital platforms. Yet, paradoxically, those strategies are enabled by cloud infrastructures provided by the same platform companies, deepening the dependence of news organizations on these companies. Thus, infrastructural integration is a process of demarcation of spaces and activities between news organizations and tech companies.
affiliations: Department of Media Studies, University of Amsterdam

latest_articles.title: War, Feelings of Belonging, and News Diets: How Russia’s Full-Scale Invasion of Ukraine Did (Not) Change the News Repertoires of Russian Speakers in Germany
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, launched in February 2022, has influenced the news repertoires of first-generation Russian-speaking migrants living in Germany. While previous research suggests that news consumption patterns are typically stable, it has also shown that major disruptive events - such as the COVID-19 pandemic - have the potential for significant shifts. However, little research has explored how wars impact the transnational news repertoires of migrant communities. Grounded in 25 semi-structured interviews, the study demonstrates that the four types of news repertoires identified by previous research on Russian speakers in Germany prior to 2022 remained valid. Although very few participants indicated that they had completely switched repertoire type, nuanced changes were observed within the four types. These changes were accompanied by a complex process of renegotiating their sense of belonging to Russia. Moreover, across the four types, there was a spike in news use in the first weeks of the full-scale war, followed by news avoidance, and a “migration” to the platform Telegram. This study advances research on diasporic news repertoires, digital war, and disinformation by showing that geopolitical crises can shape the news repertoires of transnational audiences who have feelings of belonging to actors involved in conflict.

latest_articles.title: Applying Relational Turbulence Theory to the Context of Sibling Caregiving Coordination for Ill Parent(s)
latest_articles.abstract: The current study applied the relational turbulence theory (RTT) to sibling relationships and examined both the relational and health implications of siblings’ care coordination for ill parent(s). People (N = 276) who were co-caring for ill parent(s) with at least one sibling completed an online survey to assess their perceptions of sibling relationships, communication with siblings, and caregiver burden. Data were analyzed using structural equation modeling. Results were largely consistent with the theoretical predictions of RTT. Specifically, relational uncertainty and interdependence in sibling relationships were related to cognitive and affective responses, which were associated with communicative outcomes, relational turbulence, and ultimately caregiver burden. We further explored the distinctive sibling relationship dynamics in proximal and long-distance caregiving. Multigroup analysis results revealed no significant differences in relationship dynamics between proximal and long-distance caregiving groups. Implications and limitations of the findings are discussed.

latest_articles.title: Characteristics of Suicide Typologies: Personal and Social Determinants of Suicidal Behaviors
latest_articles.abstract: = 1,797), personal factors (e.g., life satisfaction, happiness, psychological distress, suicide-related perception, and attitude) and social factors (i.e., frequent exposure to suicide messages via traditional and social media, interpersonal communication with family, friends, and health care professionals, the quality and quantity of social support) are examined to identify multifaceted characteristics of suicide typologies. As a result of a series of latent profile analyses, an eight-latent profile model is determined. It is also found that suicidal behaviors (i.e., intention and attempt) significantly differ depending on suicide typologies.

latest_articles.title: How does young children’s digital resilience operate within and across homes and communities? A thematic analysis of parents and early years educators’ experiences
latest_articles.abstract: This paper examines how young children aged 0–5 years build digital resilience within interconnected home and community contexts. While playing, exploring, and socialising are central to early experiential learning, little is known about how parents/carers and educators support children to recognise, manage, and recover from mistakes in connected environments. Conceptualising digital resilience as a socio-ecological construct, the paper draws on findings from the TYKES project to address this gap. Using a multi-method qualitative design, the study thematically analyses semi-structured interviews with parents/carers (n = 17) and early years educators (n = 5), alongside focus groups with educators across two settings (n = 8), conducted using purposive sampling over a ten-month period (May 2024–February 2025). The paper argues that digital resilience is a relational and context-dependent process that unfolds across nested home and community environments, rather than solely within individual children or discrete settings. It highlights the importance of social capital and everyday interactions in shaping children’s emerging capacities to navigate online challenges. The paper contributes to the literature by demonstrating how parents/carers and educators actively cultivate digital resilience as an emergent capability, embedded in socio-ecological relations. The findings point to the need for more holistic and coordinated support across education systems, policymakers, industry, and governments to enable young children to thrive on the Internet.

latest_articles.title: Attitude Orients READINESS: What CEO Humility Signals to Investors in a Crisis
latest_articles.abstract: Grounded in the crisis attitude construct and the READINESS framework, this study provides initial empirical evidence that CEO-expressed humility shapes investor appraisals, emotions, and relational orientation in a crisis. Humility is theorized as a cognitive and relational grounding mechanism that supports ethical leadership under crisis pressure and functions as an authentically expressed signal from which stakeholders construe meaning—above all, trustworthiness, itself an indicator of perceived ethical leadership. In a 2 × 2 (CEO-expressed humility × organizational crisis responsibility) between-subjects online experiment (N = 79), investors exposed to higher CEO-expressed humility reported significantly greater goal congruence, stronger perceptions of CEO trustworthiness and commitment to the CEO-investor relationship, and lower anger and fear. No interaction effects reached significance, indicating humility’s relational benefits do not appear contingent on organizational fault—challenging common conceptions of humility as fit only for seeking forgiveness and supporting its characterization as a stable leader orientation rather than a situational concession. CEO-expressed humility did not significantly affect perceived communicative assertiveness, suggesting humility need not be traded against expected leader strength in crisis. Theoretical contributions to the crisis attitude construct and READINESS framework, and practical implications for ethical CEO crisis communication are discussed.

latest_articles.title: Institutional Channels Over Social Media: Digital Risk Communication, Community Engagement, and Protective Behavior Adoption Among Young Adults in a Pandemic Context
latest_articles.abstract: Young adults are widely assumed to engage primarily with health information through social media during public health crises, yet this assumption has rarely been tested empirically within institutional contexts. This study applied the Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) framework to examine how digital platforms influence protective behavior adoption among young adults during the COVID-19 pandemic. Using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) on data from an online survey of 1,185 adults recruited through a U.S. university network, we tested a four-construct model comprising community engagement, risk communication, risk perception, and adopted protective behavior. Results indicate that community engagement significantly influenced both risk perception (β = 0.425) and risk communication (β = 0.521), each of which independently enhanced protective behavior adoption. Indirect pathway analysis confirmed that both risk communication (β = 0.110) and risk perception (β = 0.129) mediated the relationship between community engagement and protective behavior. Contrary to prevailing assumptions, participants relied primarily on university e-mails (25.53%) and official websites (19.35%) for COVID-19 information, with social media playing a secondary role. These findings suggest that institutional communication channels represent a distinct and undertheorized mediating variable in RCCE models and should be explicitly incorporated into public health communication frameworks for future health emergencies.

latest_articles.title: The news production circuit: Tracing the implementation of constructive journalism
latest_articles.abstract: Constructive journalism is increasingly invoked in newsroom strategies, educational programs, and professional debates. Yet scholarship has struggled to account for how constructive ambitions are implemented in practice over time. Existing research tends to cluster around partially disconnected domains – such as professional discourse, newsroom initiatives, and content and audience effects – without specifying the dynamic, on-going processes that link organizational decisions to editorial action and the resulting news products. This conceptual article addresses that gap by introducing an analytical framework – the MAP model (Mechanics, Actions, Products) – that conceptualizes implementation as recurring production pathways connecting organizational conditions, situated newswork, and published output. Implementation relies on sustaining these pathways through feedback loops that carry evaluations back into subsequent cycles of production. A pathway may be reinforced and repeated or left unsupported and abandoned, depending on whether the output’s value is registered and recognized. Together, these domains and processes constitute the news production circuit. The article demonstrates the analytical value of MAP through three distinct implementation configurations derived from recent research on constructive journalism. In doing so, it provides a vocabulary for comparative research on how journalistic practices, more generally, are implemented – and for identifying where and why implementation remains partial, uneven, or fragile.

latest_articles.title: Dependence or Interdependence? A Folk-Theories Perspective on Journalists’ and Activists’ Mutual Perceptions
latest_articles.abstract: Drawing on folk theories , this study explores how mutual perceptions and experiences shape the journalist–activist relationship. We analyze data from two German interview studies: activists from diverse protest movements ( N = 33) and journalists covering them ( N = 38). Both groups tend to hold simplified views of each other’s work yet apply similar criteria when evaluating “good” journalism/activism and affirm the importance of their roles for democracy. Conflicts often arise from unmet expectations. The study offers insights into how journalism is understood in movement contexts and vice versa. It also clarifies the recently debated boundaries between journalism and activism.
affiliations: GESIS Leibniz Institute for the Social Science, Mannheim, Germany

latest_articles.title: Can AI Gauge Deliberative Quality? Evaluating Deliberation on Social Media With Large Language Models
latest_articles.abstract: Although social media has become a central arena for deliberative discourse, debates are frequently characterized by incivility. Due to the volume of online discourse, it is challenging to assess when and where interventions, such as community-based counterspeech, are required. Accordingly, automated measurement of deliberative quality is a powerful tool for facilitating constructive online communication. Since deliberation is multidimensional, attempts to monitor online discourse must consider alternative forms of communication to foster inclusive deliberation. Whereas Type I deliberative dimensions, such as rationality and civility, are grounded in Habermasian ideals, Type II deliberation extends this perspective by incorporating alternative communicative forms, including emotionality and storytelling, into a more inclusive assessment of deliberative quality. Addressing the limitations of prior studies that primarily focused on classic Type I deliberative dimensions and tested only a small number of large language models, this study evaluates multiple open-weight models to conduct a nuanced assessment of deliberative quality. We applied the large language model that achieved the best overall balance between predictive performance, model size, and computational efficiency to a dataset of 64,223 comments from German-language climate change discourse on X. Our results demonstrate that large language models can reliably capture complex Type II deliberative dimensions despite class imbalances and subtle linguistic cues that generally hinder automated text classification. Class imbalance often impairs classification performance due to highly skewed label distributions, and Type II dimensions are particularly difficult to detect as they are often signaled by implicit, context-dependent markers. The empirical analysis also reveals distinct communicative patterns: While public speakers predominantly employ civil, rational, constructive, and common-good-oriented communication, other debating users exhibit higher levels of reciprocal engagement, humor, and negative emotions, alongside more frequent incivility. Our study demonstrates that AI-driven measurement can serve as a foundational tool for identifying norm violations, directing counterspeech toward specific debates, promoting inclusive digital public spheres, and observing broader long-term effects of moderation and interventions on the quality of debate.

latest_articles.title: Monitoring Electoral Democracy: Discovering and Reusing Text and Multimedia Data for Political Communication Research
latest_articles.abstract: Political communication research relies on a fragmented landscape of media sources, text and multimedia corpora, analytical tools, and research workflows. Researchers face two related barriers: identifying which resources exist and determining whether and under what conditions they can be accessed and reused. This article presents Monitoring Electoral Democracy (MEDem), a distributed European research infrastructure for comparative political communication research, with particular attention to its Service Center for Text and Multimedia Data. The Service Center develops two complementary services: MEDem Meteor provides a curated, knowledge-graph-based discovery layer that connects media sources, datasets, archives, analytical tools, and publications; MEDem Amsterdam Content Analysis Toolkit supports the hosting, controlled reuse, and non-consumptive analysis of text and multimedia corpora. Together, the services address discovery and access as interconnected infrastructural problems. MEDem Meteor makes dispersed resources, relationships, and coverage gaps visible, while MEDem Amsterdam Content Analysis Toolkit makes access conditions transparent and enables reuse without redistributing protected content. This combination can reduce duplicated data collection, support more theoretically informed source selection, and strengthen cumulative and comparative research. Its realization, however, depends on sustained curation, community participation, and long-term institutional commitment.

latest_articles.title: ‘Dirty work’ in UK television: Ancillary work and the grey zones of creative labour
latest_articles.abstract: UK television ancillary workers, the cleaners, drivers, caterers and security staff who service television productions, occupy a paradoxical position: essential, yet routinely excluded from conceptions of the creative workforce and subjected to inferior working conditions, status and recognition. Drawing on an in-depth mixed-methods study, we argue that specialised ancillary workers should be recognised as part of the television production workforce and given scholarly and industry attention. We apply the sociological concept of ‘dirty work’ to creative labour, adapting it into our understanding of the ‘grey zones’ of creative work: marginalised, peripheral forms of work overlooked by academic and policy frameworks. We engage with media and cultural industries approaches to show how a narrow focus on those designated ‘creative’ workers reproduces existing class hierarchies. The article calls for a broader, more inclusive research agenda as a matter of social justice and scholarly responsibility. The findings highlight pervasive issues faced by ancillary workers, including long hours, low pay, lack of basic amenities and lack of respect, alongside their own perspectives and identity work. Excluding ancillary work from the creative labour paradigm is analytically and ethically flawed, and we propose an expanded framework that values all labour in the production process.
affiliations: TV Industry Human Rights Forum, London, UK

latest_articles.title: The managed sisterhood: Gendered labor and intimacy in Chinese fashion influencer industry
latest_articles.abstract: As China’s leading multi-channel network (MCN) institutions become increasingly industrialized and bureaucratic, their operations are paradoxically characterized by intensified emotional dynamics. Drawing on ethnographic research within a women-dominated fashion influencer team, this study identifies a sisterhood-based production model that embeds sisterly ties within hierarchical organizational structures. It traces the formation and collapse of this managed sisterhood. By cultivating an illusion of unity and belonging, intimacy makes labor more governable, obscuring coercion while facilitating the mobilization of emotional, aesthetic, and physical capacities. In this way, sisterhood becomes integral to production, intensifying labor and rendering precarity routine. Under platform capitalism, traditional Chinese sisterhood, once grounded in kinship and flexible resistance, is reconfigured into an occupational form of informal labor control, producing “disposable kinship” in which affective bonds become temporary and replaceable. This study challenges dominant political readings of sisterhood and demonstrates how intimacy itself becomes a mechanism of governance within platform capitalism.
affiliations: Renmin University of China, Beijing, China

latest_articles.title: When Are Low Person-Centered Support Messages Effective and Appropriate? A Qualitative Validation and Revision of the LPC Message Effectiveness Model
latest_articles.abstract: The recently proposed LPC Message Effectiveness Model established the conditions when recipients may perceive LPC messages as less harmful or potentially effective. Our study uses qualitative analyses to identify aspects of the model that should be revised or expanded, including considering how both relational closeness and distance may work in favor of LPC messages, expanding the mediator variable goodwill to the broader concept of credibility, and adding expectancy violations and confirmations as an influence on perceived message accuracy. We also specify that, for some people, no one can communicate LPC messages effectively, thus creating a boundary for the model.

latest_articles.title: Digital transformation in Public Service Media: Adaptation strategies of European broadcasters
latest_articles.abstract: Public Service Media (PSM) are currently undergoing a structural transformation driven by the digitalization of the media ecosystem. Audience fragmentation, the emergence of multi-platform environments and the growing centrality of digital platforms are compelling public service broadcasters to rethink their organizational models, editorial practices and content distribution strategies. This article examines how different European PSM organizations are responding to these challenges and explores how digital transition processes are contributing to the redefinition of the role of PSM in contemporary media systems. The study draws on a comparative analysis of five public service operators – British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC, the United Kingdom), RTÉ (Ireland), RTBF (Belgium), Radiotelevisión Española (RTVE, Spain),and RTP (Portugal) – supported by semi-structured interviews with key institutional actors and a systematic review of strategic reports, concession contracts and regulatory documents produced between 2018 and 2025. The findings reveal that, despite national specificities, several convergent trends are emerging, including the growing importance of digital platforms, the reorganization of production structures into convergent and cross-media models, and the redefinition of public service missions in a media environment shaped by platformization and intensified informational competition. The article argues that digital transformation does not diminish the relevance of PSM; on the contrary, it reinforces their importance as critical infrastructures for trustworthy information, cultural diversity and democratic cohesion.

latest_articles.title: Calls to action and voter engagement on Facebook: a comparative study of eight European election campaigns
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines the use of Facebook by political actors across eight European countries – Czech Republic, Germany, Hungary, Kosovo, Norway, Portugal, Spain, United Kingdom – as they attempt to engage voters through calls to action. By analysing what is often referred to as the supply and demand of political communication, the paper conceptualizes three primary types of calls to action: informing, mobilizing, and interacting. Our findings reveal that mobilizing calls are the most prevalent, reflecting the central mission of election campaigns to secure voter turnout. However, such calls do not necessarily result in higher user engagement compared to informative content. Despite the potential for interactive features to enhance dialogic communication, they remain underutilized, with political actors apparently favouring controlled interactivity to maintain message control. The study highlights significant cross-country differences, with variations in the degree of engagement reached by different calls to action as influenced by national political contexts and campaign cultures. The research underscores the importance of considering both the strategic priorities of political actors and the cultural and institutional factors that shape voter engagement on social media.
affiliations: CITCEM – Transdisciplinary Research Centre “Culture, Space and Memory”, University of Porto

latest_articles.title: An integrated national image scale: Combining nation, structural relations and emotion dimensions
latest_articles.abstract: This study aims to provide an updated, comprehensive and systematic national image scale in a context where the ways states behave and the criteria people use to evaluate foreign nations may have transformed. By integrating concepts and measurements from various social science fields, including international relations, political psychology and communication, we developed a multidimensional conceptual framework and operationalisation of national image, consisting of three dimensions: nation, structural relations and emotion. Taking China's national image as a case study and conducting large-scale cross-national surveys ( N = 3, 600), our findings demonstrated that the normative sub-dimension of a nation and three components of the emotion dimension have universally influenced the foreign public attitudes towards China. Meanwhile, the impact of the structural relations dimensions on national image is highly context-dependent. Finally, the policy implications are discussed.

latest_articles.title: In need of transnational news literacies: What migrant audiences from an autocracy know about their news
latest_articles.abstract: Extant news-literacy research has focused mainly on democracies and nationwide populations. By contrast, we know little about migrants’ news literacy knowledge. To address this gap, we present a case study grounded in 42 semi-structured interviews with Russian speakers who migrated from authoritarian post-Soviet contexts to democratic Germany. The study describes a phenomenon we conceptualise as ‘transnational news literacy’, understood as the stocks of knowledge a group needs to critically evaluate information received across several news environments. The results illustrate how this knowledge differed significantly among interviewees in two major elements of news literacy: (1) the creation and (2) the context of news. When participants lacked knowledge of specific elements, they often relied on broadly available symbolic resources – conceptualised in the study as ‘folk theories’ – which they applied across both news environments. The paper also discusses the practical implications for news literacy programs developed for migrant audiences.
affiliations: Bavarian Research Institute for Digital Transformation
Department of Political Communication with a Focus on Eastern Europe and the Post-Soviet Region, University of Passau

latest_articles.title: Building and Maintaining Trust in AI Chatbots: Introducing Generative Information Retrieval Accountability Assessment Framework (GIRAAF)
latest_articles.abstract: Social integration of AI requires public trust and appropriate governance. This paper introduces the Generative Information Retrieval Accountability Assessment Framework (GIRAAF), designed to appraise accountability for Large Language Models and their applications, including AI chatbots. Drawing on Dahl’s (1998) notion of enlightened citizens, the framework comprises six interlinked dimensions: Information Readiness, Factual Correctness, Normative Alignment, Sourcing Practice, Transparency and Explainability, and Responsiveness and Adaptivity. Together, these dimensions link observable text outputs to intelligible standards, enabling systematic evaluation and accountable oversight. For scholars, developers and policymakers, GIRAAF provides a diagnostic heuristic and shared vocabulary for critical analysis of AI chatbot performance.

latest_articles.title: Positioning enjoyment and appreciation as key components of news use
latest_articles.abstract: In response to the continued convergence and hybridization of news and entertainment media content, this research explores the roles of enjoyment and appreciation in contemporary news use. Three studies (two surveys and one experiment) show a clear link between enjoyment, appreciation, and news use. Both enjoyment and appreciation are positively related to agreement, value alignment, attitude change, and attitude reinforcement in the context of news use. News enjoyment is related to increased positive and decreased negative emotions, while news appreciation is connected to an increase in and tolerance of mixed emotions. Importantly, news enjoyment decreases actual knowledge while facilitating greater affective polarization. News appreciation increases more positive feelings toward other people. These results illustrate the value of merging research on entertainment and news media, and they also suggest that news enjoyment is a driving factor in the growth of less democratic news use outcomes.
affiliations: Brian Lamb School of Communication, Purdue University , West Lafayette, IN,
Department of Communication, University of Tampa, Tampa, FL, United States

latest_articles.title: The democratic value of local information: How journalistic and non-journalistic sources relate to community attachment, civic engagement, and democratic attitudes
latest_articles.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between local information use, community integration, and political attitudes within the German context. Drawing on representative survey data from 2069 citizens, we examine how using journalistic and non-journalistic local information sources, specifically official municipal sources, community-based sources and interpersonal communication, relates to community attachment, civic engagement, satisfaction with local democracy, and trust in local politics. Results indicate that, consistent with previous scholarship, frequent local media use is positively associated with stronger community attachment, higher civic engagement, and more favorable evaluations of local politics and local democracy. Compared to non-journalistic sources of information, local media emerged as stronger predictors of community attachment, satisfaction with local democracy, and trust in local politics, but not civic engagement. Our findings highlight the need for closer examination of how the growing diversity of local information sources impact community integration and civic engagements in an increasingly hybrid media environment.
affiliations: Department of Media and Communication, University of Erfurt

latest_articles.title: Invisible Women in Economics: Almost Two Centuries of Gender Representation in the Financial Times and The Economist (1843–2021)
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines gender representation in the Financial Times and The Economist between 1843 and 2021. Using millions of articles and name-frequency analysis, it traces the long-term evolution of women’s visibility in economic news. Results reveal a U -shaped pattern: relatively high representation in the nineteenth century, a decline through much of the 20th century, and a gradual recovery since the 1980s. Comparisons with benchmarks of women’s participation in high-status occupations and economic sectors show a persistent gap between media visibility and real-world presence. The findings point to a lasting paper ceiling in economic journalism. JEL codes: J16, N34, L82
affiliations: University of Modena and Reggio Emilia, Italy

latest_articles.title: With a Little Help From AI?! Governing Visual Hate Speech Through AI-Assisted Counter-Image Practices
latest_articles.abstract: The attention-grabbing and memorable nature of visuals makes them a powerful vehicle for spreading hate online. As platforms increasingly reconsider or scale back content moderation efforts, user-centered interventions are gaining importance as complementary governance strategies. While prior research demonstrates the effectiveness of empathy-based textual counter speech, little is known about the role of visual counter speech in mitigating hateful imagery. This preregistered study examines the effectiveness of user-centered interventions against visual hate speech. Using an experimental design ( N = 666), we tested four interventions against a no-intervention control condition in response to hateful images targeting transgender persons: (a) empathy-based textual counter speech, (b) AI-generated generic counter images, (c) AI-generated specific counter images replicating elements of the original, and (d) platform-issued warning labels. Results show substantial variation across interventions. Empathy-based textual counter speech and AI-generated specific counter images showed the most consistent reductions in amplification-oriented behaviors, particularly forwarding. Visual interventions did not outperform textual counter speech, suggesting that effectiveness depends less on modality and more on the specificity and contextual alignment of the intervention. Furthermore, effectiveness varied with the intensity of the hate content. Interventions were most effective for humor-based, more ambiguously harmful content, whereas their impact diminished for more severe forms of hate. The consistent performance of AI-generated specific counter images further points to the potential of generative AI to provide users with a rapid, low-cost, and accessible means of producing context-sensitive counter speech.

latest_articles.title: Attitudes Toward LGB and TGD Rights in Latin America
latest_articles.abstract: Research on attitudes toward transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) individuals lags behind research on opinion on the lesbian, gay, and bisexual (LGB) population, leaving open questions about public opinion on these two LGBTQ+ subgroups, in general and in particular in the Global South. While a sizeable gap exists in US public opinion toward TGD and LGB rights, we do not know whether that finding is generalizable to other contexts. With a focus on Latin America, we draw on a range of scholarship to identify factors that could result in a similar divergence of attitudes toward these subgroups or, instead, relative convergence. Our analyses focus primarily on novel survey data from representative surveys across thirteen Latin American countries. Our results demonstrate a fair amount of convergence in mean levels, item nonresponse rates, and predictors of views on LGB versus TGD rights. We present some notable differences across countries and issues, with results for the former (countries) varying by socio-political context and the latter (issues) varying across political and nonpolitical domains. We identify these patterns as constituting a future agenda for researchers of opinion on LGBTQ+ topics. We conclude that, in the contemporary period, the Latin American public holds fairly similar mental schemas toward LGB and TGD groups.

latest_articles.title: How the Public Makes Sense of Gender Politics: Textual, Emotional, and Symbolic Dimensions
latest_articles.abstract: How do ordinary citizens make sense of gender politics? While research has examined public support for feminism and gender equality either separately or as interchangeable concepts, far less is known about the meanings citizens attach to these labels and whether they evoke distinct political meanings. This article compares the textual, emotional, and symbolic associations of three related but distinct framings of gender politics: feminism, gender equality, and equality between men and women. Drawing on an original pre-registered survey experiment in Spain, respondents were randomly assigned to define and evaluate one of the three labels, allowing us to analyze their meanings across textual, emotional, and visual dimensions. We find that while most respondents express sympathy toward all three labels, feminism stands as the most contested. Feminism also has the sharpest sociopolitical profile, eliciting greater support from young, highly educated, progressive women. Text analyses reveal that the public frames feminism in terms of collective action, conflict, and women’s identity, drawing heavily on political language, while the other two labels emphasize policy and material concerns. Emotionally, gender politics elicits more positive than negative responses across all three labels, though men report slightly higher negative emotions toward feminism. Feminism is also the only label consistently associated with images of women’s mobilization and protest, reinforcing its distinctively political resonance. These findings show that feminism and gender equality tap related but meaningfully distinct constructs in the public mind, with implications for how scholars measure attitudes toward gender politics and interpret public support for equality-related policies.

latest_articles.title: Red, White & Royal Blue : incorporating queer intimacy into the nation
latest_articles.abstract: Red, White & Royal Blue (RWRB) follows the love story and coming-out narratives of Alex Claremont-Diaz, the bisexual Mexican American son of the U.S. President, and Henry Fox, the gay white British prince who is third in line for the throne. This article examines RWRB as a romantic comedy that offers insight into the contemporary relationship between surveillance, national identity, and queer intimacy. Using queer surveillance as an analytical lens, I develop incorporation as a surveillance operation to describe how queer intimacy becomes visible and politically useful for national narratives of social progress. Romantic comedy offers audiences optimistic representations of “the good life” that fold queer intimacy into that fantasy under homonational conditions. I trace this incorporation through three interlocking surveillance operations: containing racial difference, disciplining sex, and rendering queer identities transparent.

latest_articles.title: “I’m a biracial person who looks white in a Black man’s rap game”: exploring expressions of multiracialized masculine vulnerability in Logic’s “Everybody”
latest_articles.abstract: The field of Black vulnerability studies includes analyses of Black men rap artists’ sexual debut, romantic relationships, mental stress, self-medication, and suicidal thoughts. I expand this analysis to Black-white mixed-race men who express emotional vulnerability regarding their racial identities. Using a case study of the song “Everybody” by Logic—a Black and white, mixed-race man—I find that Logic expresses joy and pride in his Black and biracial identity. Similarly, I observe that he expresses anger and frustration toward those who question, dismiss, or degrade his Black and biracial identities, a pattern paralleled in research on multiracial individuals. By analyzing his radio and website interviews, along with his personal video log (vlog) to contextualize and supplement the textual analysis of “Everybody,” I argue that Logic’s portrayal of a multiracialized masculine vulnerability in his music presents a complex and layered emotional response to challenges to his racial identity. Consequently, this research expands the literature on Black male vulnerability to include Black-white multiracial men in rap.
affiliations: Sociology and Anthropology, University of Richmond, Richmond, VA, USA

latest_articles.title: The Effectiveness of Narrative Messages for Promoting End-of-Life Communication
latest_articles.abstract: Engaging in an end-of-life (EOL) conversation with a close other has multiple advantages, yet persuading individuals to have an EOL conversation remains a challenge. We examined how narrative messages shape attitudes and behavioral intentions to initiate an EOL conversation compared to informational messages. We conducted an online experiment using a between-subjects design with four conditions: (a) a narrative with role modeling, (b) a narrative without role modeling, (c) information-only, and (d) no-message control. All message conditions produced more favorable EOL attitudes than the no-message control, whereas only narratives produced higher EOL behavioral intentions. The role modeling effect was not supported in the current study. Transportation and identification were positively associated with EOL attitudes and EOL behavioral intentions, although only transportation statistically significantly predicted behavioral intentions in a regression including both variables. Findings suggested that narrative messages may be especially useful for motivating intentions to initiate difficult conversations.
affiliations: University at Buffalo, Buffalo, New York, USA

latest_articles.title: Words That Heal: A Systematic Review of Healthcare Providers–Patient Communication to Enhance Chronic Care Management and Practice Recommendations
latest_articles.abstract: Chronic diseases represent a major global health burden, and suboptimal treatment adherence remains a key obstacle to long-term management. Healthcare provider (HCP)–patient communication is a modifiable determinant of adherence and psychological functioning, yet evidence remains fragmented across conditions and communication domains. This review builds on patient-centered communication scholarship and established models of communication functions and pathways linking clinician-patient communication to health outcomes. This systematic review synthesizes empirical evidence on HCP–patient communication strategies associated with treatment adherence and psychological outcomes among adults with chronic diseases, including diabetes, cancer, cardiovascular, and respiratory conditions. Following PRISMA guidelines and PROSPERO registration (CRD42020171690), five databases (Scopus, PubMed, PsycINFO, Cochrane Library, Google Scholar) were searched. Results: Twenty-seven studies met the inclusion criteria. Communication strategies clustered into four macro-domains: (1) trust and interpersonal relationship; (2) information exchange and decision processes; (3) active involvement, empowerment, and autonomy; and (4) change processes, emotional regulation, and management of difficulties. Domains were defined a priori from patient-centered communication, self-management, and behavior-change literature and refined during data extraction. Across conditions, integrated communication patterns addressing multiple domains were generally associated with favorable adherence, self-management, clinical, quality-of-life, and healthcare-utilization outcomes, although evidence strength varied by study design, disease context, and methodological quality. Findings support a provisional, evidence-informed framework in which HCP–patient communication strategies, organized within relational, informational, participatory, and change-regulatory macro-domains, may engage proximal regulatory processes that, in turn, may be associated with adherence and other chronic-care outcomes. Prospective studies are needed to test these pathways.

latest_articles.title: “A Minefield for the Novice”: Australian Women’s Experiences Seeking Health Information Online About Perimenopause
latest_articles.abstract: During perimenopause, many women experience psychological and physiological symptoms that can seriously impact quality of life and future health. However, they report challenges accessing appropriate information and medical support, likely exacerbated by clinician knowledge gaps, stigma, and a persistent lack of research, consistent with a documented pattern of structural sexism in health systems. Consequently, women increasingly turn to alternative sources, particularly online, for support. Although scholarship exists on online health-information seeking and women's digital health engagement, limited research examines how women navigate online health information under clinical and structural invalidation. This study gathered responses from 58 perimenopausal women through an online qualitative survey and constructed three themes using reflexive thematic analysis: (a) the search for validation; (b) trust erosion and the support gap; and (c) self-efficacy, agency and kinship. Interpreted through an epistemic injustice lens, the findings indicated that participants used digital literacy strategies to reassert epistemic standing and compensate for structural lack of support, yet were left to navigate variable-quality health information. Therefore, health information providers and policymakers should acknowledge perimenopausal complexity, model knowledge-appraisal strategies rather than present information as resolved, and mandate training to address the support gap. Health professionals should also validate women's epistemic standing before clinically interpreting symptoms.

latest_articles.title: Negotiating exit: Career mobility and institutional status premium among young journalists in China’s mainstream media
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how young journalists in China’s mainstream media negotiate career exit amid structural and technological change. Drawing on a constructivist grounded theory approach and 30 in-depth interviews with former journalists aged 35 or younger across China’s four-tier media system, we identify three interconnected concepts that shape how mobility decisions take form. First, the erosion of professional values, rooted in blurred editorial–commercial boundaries, dual-track personnel stratification, and declining social recognition, generates cumulative dissatisfaction. Second, peer comparison makes alternative career paths visible and desirable through exposure to peers’ successful transitions. Third, institutional status premium, the non-transferable symbolic capital, social recognition, and resource access tied to state-affiliated media membership, anchors journalists by raising the perceived cost of leaving. These forces do not operate uniformly. Participants from central-level media reported stronger institutional constraints and higher perceived exit costs than those from lower-level media. Older cohorts attribute greater weight to institutional status, while younger journalists, particularly the post-95 generation, place markedly less emphasis on it. Exit thus emerges not as a direct response to a single pressure but as a delayed, negotiated outcome shaped by the convergence of dissatisfaction, opportunity, and constraint. By demonstrating how these forces interact and how constraints are unevenly distributed across hierarchies and generations, the study challenges static, factor-based explanations and advances a process-oriented account of career mobility in an institutionally distinctive context.

latest_articles.title: Participatory journalism in practice: Assessing interactivity and citizen contributions in newsrooms
latest_articles.abstract: Digital news organisations offer audiences multiple opportunities to comment, share, submit information, and engage with journalists, but these mechanisms do not necessarily redistribute editorial authority. This article examines how interactivity enables, channels, and constrains citizen participation across the news production process. It combines a conceptual literature review, a comparative synthesis of 20 studies published between 1999 and 2025, a case analysis of The Washington Post , National Post , and The Guardian , and six written semi-structured interviews with journalists. The findings show that participation is concentrated in Access/Observation, Distribution, and Interpretation, with more limited involvement in Selection/Filtering, while Processing/Editing remains under stronger professional control. The article develops a qualitative evaluation model that distinguishes selective, communicative, and productive interactivity according to production stage, citizen agency, and implications for editorial authority. It argues that participatory journalism is best understood as managed openness: news organisations widen opportunities for citizen involvement while retaining control over the institutional core of news production, contributing to broader debates on digital participation and media power.
affiliations: Department of Communication Sciences, Universidade Europeia, Lisbon, Portugal
Instituto de História Contemporânea (IHC), IN2PAST, Universidade NOVA de Lisboa, Lisbon, Portugal

latest_articles.title: Guardians of the cyberverse: Dispositional, attitudinal, and autobiographical correlates of user engagement against misogynist digital hate
latest_articles.abstract: As digital misogyny remains widespread, user intervention is an essential complement to lenient platform governance. Yet, willingness to intervene varies considerably across individuals and cultural contexts. In a cross-national survey conducted in Austria ( n = 791), France ( n = 800), Hungary ( n = 775), and Sweden ( n = 785), we examine how dispositional, attitudinal, and autobiographical characteristics relate to users’ direct and indirect intervention and support for moderation. Empathic anger consistently emerged as the strongest positive predictor of all three outcomes across countries. Perspective-taking, online self-presentation, and victimization experiences showed meaningful positive associations with intervention, while misogynist attitudes were inconsistently related. Toxic disinhibition showed a dual pattern, negatively associated with moderation support but positively associated with direct intervention across all countries, suggesting its potential to be cleverly repurposed toward counterspeech. These findings underscore the importance of emotionally activating literacy programs and highlight the need for culturally sensitive intervention models.

latest_articles.title: Drenched in blue: Black audiences’ TV viewing and perceptions of the police
latest_articles.abstract: Amid conversation about police conduct, understanding the mechanisms that may be related to Black audiences’ police procedural consumption and attitudes toward the police is noteworthy. Accordingly, we adopted social identity gratifications theory to analyze survey data from US Black adults (N = 434) regarding consumption of Black police procedurals, scripted shows focused on police investigations with Black actors, and attitudes toward the police. Results suggest a significant relationship between increased consumption and favorable attitudes toward the police. However, data indicated that adherence to racial identity moderated the relationship, acting as a safeguard against heavy media exposure and viewer attitudes.

latest_articles.title: Worldbuilding, otherwise, together: critical performative pedagogical encounters as pedagogical rehearsal
latest_articles.abstract: To this forum conversation, we offer the practice of critical performative pedagogical encounters (henceforth: Encounters), a community-based performance activity devised to interrogate cultural power as it courses through bodies with the intent of shifting those embodied performances toward liberatory ends. As a community practice, Encounters invites collaborative critique, communal rehearsal, and collective renewal in the move toward cultural revolution, beginning in our bodies.
